speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (for the Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: that Bill C-62, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act, the Criminal Code, the Customs Act, the Customs Thriff, the Excise Act, the Income Tax Act, the Statistics Act and the Icuc Court of Canada Act, be read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. Minister of State.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before the House today is the result of long and detailed studies and debate. It is a bridge to an equitable and prosperous future. Of course it is a tax, and of course it is unpopular, but it never will be, any more than income tax and all the other taxes introduced over the years. However, when we stop to think and consider the tremendous cost of our social programs and other services that Canadians demand, and rightly so, these taxes are necessary, and this particular tax reform, the GST, is both necessary and timely. Mr. Speaker, there is no future without a certain cost.
If we were to conduct a poll on income tax, I am sure most respondents would say they don't like income tax. Should we abolish income tax? That is the kind of logic or lack of logic being used by the opposition. Opposition members have been telling us, day after day, that the polls show that 80 per cent of Canadians don't like the idea of a tax on goods and services. According to them, Canadians are asking us to abandon this tax reform proposal. Of course, opposition members are playing on these concerns-after all, it is a major reform. People are entitled to express some concern, to have perfectly legitimate questions. However, our proposal is perfectly fair to people of modest incomes, for example, and provides assistance to small businesses in coping with this tax.
So we have answers to these questions but the opposition members, instead of acting responsibly by helping the government restore the nation's finances, take the easy course and use an unpopular tax to embarrass the government. The opposition members forget this great responsibility, especially in the present context when we
April 10, 1990

are at the end of seven years of economic growth, when the economy is slowing down and when we are faced with a national debt and a large deficit that we must fight. Instead of looking for solutions to these problems for which they are largely responsible because of their previous management, they make sport of it. What is easier than asking someone, "Are you for or against a tax? Put your name at the bottom of the page". But what does that prove? It proves nothing. I feel that our responsibilities as members of Parliament go much further.
No tax in the world, Mr. Speaker, has majority support. I saw a similar tax implemented in France, where they talked about a second French revolution, in Spain, where they talked about a major social crisis, and six weeks after the law was passed, these taxes were working very well. We are told that it will be a disaster for the tourism industry. Just see how Canadians rush to Mexico, which has a GST, a value added tax, how they go in great numbers to England, France, Italy, countries where tourism is a very important industry that works well. A balanced tax system does not prevent this- These arguments are based on a fundamental misconception, which the opposition takes pleasure in exploiting to create problems for the government.
But you know, Mr. Speaker, there are times in a government's life when it must make decisions and take initiatives that may be unpopular, I agree, but are necessary for the country's health and well-being. So when an epidemic outbreak becomes a definite possibility the government may have no choice other than prescribe vaccination for everybody. As far as I know people do not particularly care for vaccination, but that just may be necessary to protect the health and even the life of the citizenry. It so happens that economic vaccines are required now and then, and such is the case today with respect to the federal sales tax which Canadians have been paying for almost 64 years and which is nothing short of a virus gnawing at the economy. I am sure most of our colleagues on the other side agree: the current manufacturer's sales tax, ultimately paid by the consumer, simply has to go. It has been identified as a virus and the GST is the vaccine which will help us get rid of it. The existing federal sales tax is a virus against which we must fight because it strikes at the core of our
Government Orders
country's future growth and prosperity by stiffling domestic productivity and exports of Canadian made goods.
Mr. Speaker, picture if you will a major industrial country like Canada with its sparsely populated expanses, a country whose survival depends on exports and which is the only industrial nation with a tax structure having such a stupid levy that, on both domestic and international markets, Canadian producers are more handicapped than their competitors. We must do away with this aberration. This virus also undermines our efforts to lower the deficit and strengthen our budgetary process because this tax is an ever growing fester on our tax structure.
At the time of the last budget, as I said, when we increased the manufacturer's sales tax to ensure a certain level of revenue, we knew that by doing so, we were running the risk that businesses would attempt to avoid it. We said: Beware, for in a year from now, we are going to replace the current system with a value added tax system, with the hope that these businesses would not make drastic changes for such a short period of time, because the current tax which concerns only some businesses and applies to 75,000 items with 22,000 exceptions is a tax which is harmful, negative, unbalanced and which encourages evasion. Well, we want to replace it to consolidate the government's basic revenues and help finance the programs which Canadians have every right to expect.
Finally, the current tax is a virus we want to get rid of because its victims are the most vulnerable in our society, because it is a silent killer of jobs, because it destroys the ability of our industries to compete, and because it reduces the productivity of our labour force. It is harmful to our economy in a world where competitiveness is of prime importance and where other economic blocks and countries are not prepared to give us a free ride.
Mr. Speaker, the necessary vaccine against the current manufacturer's sales tax which has been identified as a virus is the goods and services tax. Judging from the reaction we get from the opposition at the mere mention of this tax, we get the impression that the GST is truly an abomination, although 48 modern countries, including many of our main competitors, have implemented a similar tax. Therefore, we cannot be accused of having an overactive imagination. We have looked at other

April 10, 1990
Government Orders
alternatives. We have considered personal income taxes, where the government collects moneys straight from the people's pockets, allowing them little choice, as well as the pros and cons of a consumer's tax. We have accepted the notion that a consumer's tax could be regressive unless accompanied with several measures aimed at protecting those with limited resources.
This tax we are planning to introduce will liberate in some way the economic forces of our country. It is part of a plan this conservative government adopted when it first came to power in 1984 designed to stream line our economy and act as a positive factor to liberate the forces with are found in our businesses in Canada, and I am referring to our labour force. Our exporters and businesses will then be able to compete. It will be a solid basis for eliminating the scourge of the deficit. Our main sources of revenue include income, excise and corporate taxes as well as the leaky and unbalanced manufacturers' sales tax, which encourages evasion, applies only to certain products and creates all sorts of inequalities. By eliminating this tax which is getting increasingly difficult to collect, we will fight the deficit. It will make the Canadian economy stronger by injecting into it $9 billion, particularly in the Atlantic and Western provinces which are quite dependent on the export of natural resources.
By removing these pressures on our economy and releasing these new investments and development incentives that will benefit all Canadians, we will spread the wealth, increase public revenue through income and corporate taxes and thus fight the deficit. Mr. Speaker, this tax will guarantee a more equitable future for the most vulnerable members of our society.
During this long drawn-out debate-I will remind our friends opposite that, in the last campaign, many of my colleagues on this side of the House showed me the paper they published at that time about this reform we were proposing.
We discussed this proposal in detail in our White Paper and in our Budget documents. When pushed to the limit, the opposition has said: Sure, we understand, but we are a federal country and now we will have two levels of sales tax. And when we finished arguing that
aspect, they went across the country, saying: Not only the poor will be affected!
From the outset, we said that we wanted to make this a national tax. We discussed the tax with the provinces for two years. We knew right away this reform would not be popular, because in the past 50 years, despite any number of commissions of inquiry and reports, not a single government could bring itself to deal with the problem. Well, Mr. Speaker, we decided to deal with this problem, but the provinces, with a sales tax that was better organized than our present sales tax, could afford to say: Well, we are not going to be very popular if we go along with this. They were more reluctant and were not under the same pressures as we were. Because of the harmful aspects of our present tax, we were in much more of a hurry, and for the time being we have had to start the reform alone, but we are keeping the door open for the provinces, and at the present time, senior level talks are continuing which, I hope, will lead to a genuinely national tax in the future.
Our friends opposite insisted on the status quo. Although they admitted the status quo was unacceptable, they wouldn't budge. They also did everything they could to block the tax reform. This is not new. The Liberal Party always says no. They are against free trade, and they are against tax reform. Every time we ask for cutbacks in government spending to deal with the deficit, they object to these cutbacks which are in the best interests of this country. They object to every single measure we propose. So that is nothing new. Instead of trying to improve the measures we suggest, they have concentrated on building barriers to progress. Improvements had to come from this side of the House, from enlightened members, serious workers, who drew our attention to certain aspects of the bill that could be changed for the better. In fact, we made a lot of changes-more than seventy.
So I think the opposition's attitude is rather-
Negative!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: -is a rather bizarre joke, Mr. Speaker.
Negative!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
There is a great deal of irony in all this. We have our friends in the New Democratic Party, normally great believers in democracy who have been fighting for a long time for abolition of the Senate. They
April 10, 1990

are now prepared to create one more obstacle by asking the non-elected Senate to reverse the government's democratic process. Imagine, a party that calls itself democratic! It's like countries in Eastern Europe that were literally democratic in name only.
That's true!
Shame, comrades!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: When you have to-Imagine a party that calls itself democratic, as in the German Democratic Republic! Some democracy, Mr. Speaker!
Shame, comrades!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: -a party that has a cordial entente with non-elected members to obstruct the efforts of a government elected by a solid majority of Canadians. That is really show biz, Mr. Speaker!
They are still hamming it up!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
And what about the Official Opposition? If what the New Democratic Party does is show business, Mr. Speaker, members of the Official Opposition are a bunch of actors being manipulated by the other place.
What I see before me is a real wasteland. No proposals except for general remarks such as: Soak the rich, vague remarks like that! We would like to introduce massive reform, but when you are in the government, you have to govern, and it is the Liberal Party's failure to do so which has put the finances of this country in the abysmal situation we see today-
For 20 years!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
-and we are now trying to get the country out of this situation by making difficult decisions that are both courageous and necessary.
Members on the benches opposite are offering Canadians a bunch of illusions. They are talking about a tax on luxury items, a tax on this and a tax on that. I think it is rather disconcerting to hear our opposition colleagues talking about the tax system. They would have Canadians believe that there are simple, straightforward and painless solutions to the problems associated with the present sales tax.
According to our New Democratic Party friends, all we have to do is make the corporations and the rich pay more. Actually, what they are suggesting would have a very severe impact on small and medium-size businesses
Government Orders
and the middle-class. They are the ones who are now exempt.
It is up to you to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Moreover, this reform, this approach, would add a tax burden to corporations, which would pass it on to consumers in the end. Unfortunately, they do not understand how the economy works. They are back at the time when bankers wore black coats and top hats and had fat cigars in their mouths, as we saw when we were children in rather naughty books that often came from eastern Europe. But the world has evolved.
For example, the New Democratic Party proposed alternatives. How daring! They proposed a royal commission of inquiry on the tax system. What imagination! After 50 years of study, royal commissions, parliamentary reports and so on, the New Democratic Party wants another royal commission of inquiry. How ridiculous can you get, Mr. Speaker! Now is the time for decisions. Although ridiculous, the NDP position is at least open. We cannot say as much about the tactics and approach of the Liberal Party, which cannot tell the difference between cleverness and sneakiness. They have had trouble with that for a long time. We hear the leaders or would-be leaders each giving their own solutions: One would abolish the GST, another would not, one will see after, another will see before, a third one will see in the meantime.
They see nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Meanwhile, we see how they ran the country in the past, bringing it into an extremely difficult financial situation.
We have to be wary of the Liberal Party's tricks. We remember when they told us, "Wage and price controls? Never!" right in an election campaign.
We remember that.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: A few months later, the Liberal government implemented a system of wage and price controls. The Liberal Party told us, right in the middle of an election campaign, that they would never impose an 18-cent tax on gasoline. We know what the Liberal government did a few months later, and it was not just 18 cents-it was a lot more.

Thirty cents, thirty-two cents-

April 10, 1990
Government Orders

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Today, it is the same party which is saying "not on your life" about the GST. But what does "not on your life" means coming from that side of the House? In the Liberal lexicon, it means "yes, absolutely, but we will not say so before the election". That is why, had it not been for the courage of this government, the Liberals would have dragged their feet because they are unable to face difficult decisions. We are proud to say that this is the difference between them and us.
Fortunately, these difficult and courageous measures will have an impact which may ensure that the Liberal Party will never on your life come again to power!

Mr. Speaker, the government has stated its position clearly and honestly before the Canadian people. We have taken every opportunity available to us to debate the issue, to answer questions and to provide as much information as possible to Canadians right across the country. We will continue to do so.
It is very important to be attentive to the concerns of Canadian citizens and we are going to do that. We will try to be more efficient. We have told Canadians where we stand. We have shown that we have the courage of our convictions. That is not easy. It does not give glowing results in the public opinion polls, especially when the issues one is dealing with are painful, serious and complex. We will not imitate former Liberal governments which refused to deal with the problems associated with the federal sales tax.
You know, Mr. Speaker, I am quickly coming to the conclusion that most of our Liberal colleagues believe that Canada's national bird is the ostrich, because they keep insisting that we should stick our heads in the sand and pretend that there is no problem. Well, that may be their way of governing, but it is not ours.
In fact, on the question of tax policy, as we have done on so many matters, the members of this government are willing to put their seats on the line. The stakes are high. The existing tax costs Canadians about $9 billion in lost opportunities for growth and investment. What a price to pay to maintain the status quo, but that is exactly what the Liberal Party wants us to do.
As Jonathan Swift once wrote: "There is none so blind as they that won't see." And what about our efforts to
reduce the deficit? With a list of 22,000 exemptions to the existing sales tax, which list is growing year by year, where will we find the revenue to reduce the deficit and ultimately get rid of our $350 billion national debt?
Of course the Liberal party has never worried much about debt. The simple truth is that one way or another we all have to pay our programs and services as well as for efforts to reduce the deficit. Some people would have Canadians believe otherwise. Some people, for example, our colleagues opposite want Canadians to believe that government is Santa Claus.
You doubled the debt.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: We are talking about the debt. I will remind the hon. gentleman, a debt of $200 million with a deficit of $38 billion.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: How much is it now?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
We did not even have money to pay for Old Age Security. We had to borrow $16 billion when we came in. How could we tackle the debt?
We have reversed that. Now we have a surplus of $9 billion which allows us, finally after many years of good management, to start diminishing this debt. We had to go through that process, that together with fiscal reform is the answer.
But governments have no gifts to give because the money we have comes from the people. In the same way, the national debt is not the government's debt. It is our debt, that is, the debt of every man, woman, and child in this country.
People who try to pretend otherwise might as well be selling snake oil. However, far from selling dreams to Canadians, they are inadvertently selling nightmares, nightmares of growing national deficits and debt, nightmares of shrinking economic activity, nightmares of job losses.

Contrary to our colleagues opposite, we are not trying to impress anybody. Moments of truth are rarely easy or pleasant. They are often unpopular. If Canadians should choose not to listen to or believe the government they will have the choice to turf us out at the next election.

At the very first opportunity.
April 10, 1990

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Let the people who will be tempted to do so, make no mistake about it. Whomever is in power will have to deal with these issues. Sooner or later, the government will have to find the necessary revenues to maintain our programs and services and reduce the deficit. The government is not proposing this GST because it likes taxes. The ultimate purpose of the GST is to rectify an increasingly complex situation in order to provide Canadian men and women with the best quality of life both now and into the 21st Century.
Our children.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
When we came to power first in 1984, and again in 1988, we made some firm commitments to the Canadian people. Our economic objectives were at the core of these commitments, namely streamlining the government finances in order to protect the security of the most vulnerable in our society and of future generations, while at the same time implementing an economic reform program, including the tax system, with a view to ensuring that Canada may further develop and be better able to face a more intense competition on the world markets.
The GST is one of the cornerstones of this economic program and, now hear this, we will not be sidetracked by any kind of pressure whatsoever. Mr. Speaker, we have listened carefully to the remarks and suggestions about the GST. When we formally introduced our propositions last December, they were the outcome of lengthy discussions and detailed analyses. The bill before us faithfully mirrors the additional improvements and corrections which make me prouder than ever of our legislative measure. It represents a serious and honest effort towards reform. It deserves the support of all those who do make the effort to understand the many faults of our current system, and I hope we can count on them. You did not understand. We do not expect Canadians to like the GST, after all it is a tax. Still I am convinced that most of our fellow citizens will understand that, confronted with difficult problems-
Read this morning's papers.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: -some of which seemed to be practically unsolvable, this government took a serious, responsible and fair approach.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
This is an unfair tax.
Government Orders

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Not at all. Ours will be the most equitable system of the 48 countries that have a similar tax. When time comes to make a decision-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: There is not a federation- None of the Canadian provinces wants this sales tax-

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: What has that got to do with it? Sure. But Canada has been under a federal regime for quite some time. We have ten Ministers of Finance, ten Premiers, ten tax systems, if you will. Taxes do exist, this is not a new phenomenon. It is part and parcel of both the complexity and the wealth of our country. Would you have us scrap the provincial systems so we can standardize ours?
Never have you been able to make it visible at 13.5 per cent.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: It is an unfair and hidden tax.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Anyway, when time comes to pass judgment on this government, Mr. Speaker, I feel confident that our fellow Canadians will be first to admit that we took our responsibilities and stuck to our convictions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) on a point of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if there would be unanimous consent, in view of the rather shocking speech, the minister just made, to have a couple of questions, even though the Standing Orders do not allow them? I wonder if there would a disposition to let hon. members ask questions of the minister.
The answer is no.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There is not unanimous consent.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the hon. Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Loiselle) with much interest, because I know he has been looking for quite some time at this government's problem, which is to try and sell Bill C-62, the goods and services tax, to the Canadian people. I have a lot of respect for the minister's hard and arduous work in trying to sell an absolutely unsaleable proposal.

April 10, 1990
Government Orders
Very interestingly, Mr. Speaker, when I listened to my hon. colleague, he referred to us in opposition as if we were isolated on this whole issue. I find rather regrettable that the minister does not seem to notice the thousands of people from all walks of life, from Quebec and elsewhere, who are constantly telling us they made up their own minds the GST was no good. Admittedly, Mr. Speaker, the hon. colleague may think the dozens of Liberal members from Quebec have done a good job of convincing Quebecers, more than 75 per cent of them, that the GST is no good, because government members from Quebec have remained silent on this matter. The Minister of State (Finance) and a few other people were given the responsibility of discussing the GST on occasion. I think it is particularly disturbing that instead of asking well-informed members, members who by the way they vote in the House have shown that they support the GST, to campaign in all the provinces of this country and explain why the GST is a good deal for Canadians, instead of doing that, the government has decided to spend millions of dollars to try and convince Canadians through the media, instead of through its members, that the GST is a good deal for Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, it didn't work. We watch our hockey games, and we see people saying: Hey, Marie, we are going to get a cheque every three months. Fantastic! Who are these people? What is their income? How many children do they have? On what grounds are they saying that these people will get a cheque from the government every three months, starting December 1990? What is behind all this? It's the government's strategy for talking about the present 13.5 per cent tax and never letting its members, who are supposedly convinced of the advantages of the GST, act responsibly and stop talking about Liberals and New Democrats allegedly using scare tactics and misinforming the public. It would be only normal for the government to ask its members to do that, Mr. Speaker! These are the people who are paid to do their job, who say they are convinced, who say they understand the GST. They should be asked to go from door to door and talk to Canada's senior citizens, people in the universities and people responsible for small businesses. In other words, let them do what most members have to do as part of their responsibilities: meet their constituents. And if they do that, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member and his friends to your right will realize that
Canadians are sufficiently well-informed about the GST to say: No! We don't want the GST!

As I listened to my colleague I realized that today we will have to do something which we don't often do in this place, we will have to talk about lies; we will have to talk about cowardice; we will have to talk about misrepresentation; and we will have to talk about the kinds of things the Minister of Finance was talking about in 1988, when he said: "Wilson calls Tbmer liar, coward, and defends national sales tax plan".
That is what we will have to talk about in this place today. We will have to talk about lies; we are going to have to talk about cowardice; and we are going to have to talk about misrepresentation. We are going to have to make sure that Canadians have an opportunity to decide who is lying and who are cowards-
This is terrible! I can't believe my ears!

Terrible? What is so terrible? Mr. Speaker, I listened to the hon. member, and I agree that when Mr. Wilson said to Mr. Turner that he was a liar, that he had no guts-you can see for yourself, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Wilson did not mince words in describing Mr. Turner.

I want quote again the words of the Minister of Finance when he called John Turner a liar and a coward. Regarding the national sales tax in the 1988 election campaign, we find this report: " Mr. Wilson took pains", undoubtedly it was painful for him, "to play down the effect of his controversial tax proposal on Canadians, saying 'Canadians will not pay one penny of additional tax, as a result of these measures'."
Now we have the Minister of State for Finance saying that this is going to be a deficit reduction tool, that Canadians are not going to pay one penny more, not one penny more. At the same time the hon. Minister of Finance was calling people liars, he was saying that he would not be collecting one penny more from Canadian taxpayers. Let us take a look at the tissue of deception and lies that has taken place in the last seven or eight months. Let us start with the documents of the Department of Finance itself. I think it is very important to take a look at them since my hon. colleagues to your right, Mr. Speaker, get a little nervous. I know they all
April 10, 1990

understand. I know the member for Abitibi has read all of this material produced by the Department of Finance since August of last year. I know the member for Abitibi has looked at it all. I have no doubt about that. It is a simple tax. He being a simple man would understand a simple tax.
What I want to make sure of is that we look not at what the Liberals have have said about this and not what the New Democratic Party has said about it. Let us take a look and see what the Tories have to say about their tax.
The first document I wish to refer to is entitled Goods and Services Tax: Technical Paper issued by the Hon. Michael H. Wilson, Minister of Finance, August 1989. The H incidentally stands for "hold-up", I think. In any case this document of course was a simple document dealing with the tax, just a technical paper.
What the government did was produce this other document which is entitled Goods and Services Tax, an Overview. It was issued by the Minister of Finance in August of 1989.
It is to make sure that everybody understands it.

My hon. colleague says we should try to make sure that everybody can understand it. Let us just start anywhere. Where should you start with a document, maybe just by happenstance, but at the beginning. This is what is says on the very first page: "The goods and services tax is an integral part of the government's agenda for securing Canada's economic future. Sales tax reform will achieve three important goals. The GST will contribute to the deficit reduction effort and ensure we can continue to pay for programs and services Canadians value".
Let us look at the very first statement made in this document published in August of last year by the government. "The GST will contribute to the deficit reduction-". However, our friend who calls other people liars, says: "Mr. Wilson took pains to play down
Government Orders
the effect of his controversial tax proposal saying Canadians will not pay one penny of additional tax".
This was the Hon. Michael H. Wilson saying: "Not a penny of additional tax". This is the hon. minister saying at the very same time in his document produced in August of last year: "The GST will contribute to the deficit reduction effort". Which is it?
Another thing that went on in this very same paragraph was that the government said that we can continue to pay for programs and services Canadians value. This document was published in August of last year. Let us talk about the programs that Canadians cherish and value.
For example, let us talk about programs to protect women. Maybe someone in the House, like the hon. Minister responsible for the Status of Women, would like to comment on this particular document. The words were: "to continue to pay for programs and services Canadians value". The fact is not only will he not be doing it next year, we are not doing it now. As the hon. Minister responsible for the Status of Women would know, programs have been cut.
Already the first paragraph in this document can be contested very directly on the basis of the minister himself having said: "deficit reduction" and "We are going to continue to pay for programs and services Canadians value".
Let us look at another paragraph on the very first page where it states: "The GST will improve the over-all fairness of the tax system". This is the Tory way to be fair. You collect more money from Canadian taxpayers, but you redistribute it. You go from $18.5 billion, which was projected for 1991, and you collect $22 billion or $23 billion with the 7 per cent tax. I remind hon. members that these documents were produced, of course, at 9 per cent. We want to make sure we do not misrepresent the numbers.
With respect to the notion of fairness that is alluded to in this particular paragraph, go and ask the people who are supposedly going to be helped by the fairness aspect of this system, which I assume refers to the tax credit system. The problem is that the credits are not indexed. What we will have to do is take the minister's word. The

April 10, 1990
Government Orders
minister says: "Well, from time to time, we'll index them". If the intent is from time to time to index and to be fair, why would not the government say: "We'll just index it"? That is the fair way to do it.
Even the hon. chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance understood that. He was very clear in his statements. Many members of the Conservative Party were as well.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Gloucester has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, while you were listening to the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, I was listening to my hon. friend for Abitibi saying that there are eight cabinet ministers in the House. That is indicative of how Tories count.
Hear, hear!

I know the hon. minister is worth a lot of ministers. There are two here, to be generous, and it is nice to have them here.
I want to refer again to the document produced since it will take some time to get through the process that the government set forth to be able to come forward with its goods and services tax. Again referring to the overview that was produced in August 1989 by the government, it states on the first page: "In addition to improving the
over-all fairness of the tax system, lower and modest income Canadians will be better off once the GST is in place".
As I indicated, in 1988 the Minister of Finance took some pleasure in calling the Leader of the Liberal Party a liar. I can only state-and obviously we are not attributing this particular statement to any one person; it is a government document-that that is certainly a lie. Lower and modest income Canadians will not be better off once the GST is in place. Some may be, but not all, and that is the lie.
The studies produced by Pat Grady of Global Economics and by Neil Brooks both clearly indicate that the distributional aspects of the GST that was put forward by the Department of Finance are not accurate and cannot be defended. They say that they are erroneous and flawed. In fact, unlike what is alleged in this document produced by the government, it will not be the case once the GST is in place that low and modest income Canadians will be better off. It will mean that over half of Canadians, members of families earning under $30,000, will be no better off or worse off. This is in complete contradiction to what the government alleged in August of last year.
There are differing views on what it means for families to be better off. Some will be marginally better off. Others will be marginally less well off, but a number will be affected negatively. The Minister of Finance and the Department of Finance have been aware for some time of these figures produced by Pat Grady and by Neil Brooks. They simply said that they are wrong, but the government has not challenged them on the facts.
The government has not challenged them on the basis of the model on which they base their projections. In fact, both Mr. Brooks and Mr. Grady have been very outspoken in their criticism of the methods and the base used by the Department of Finance to arrive at its very optimistic projections which most people, including the people who are going to be affected by this, disagree with.
Poor people know that sending them a cheque every three months will take money out of circulation, while imposing a tax on practically every service that they use and every product that they buy. The Department of Finance and the Department of the National Revenue have no notion of what the implications are in terms of
April 10, 1990

the implementation of this tax for low and middle income people. Just imagine what is going to happen to anybody with less than $30,000 of income.
In order to get these cheques out in December of this year, what is the department going to base its information on? Is it going to take numbers out of the air or just conjure up a number? No. It is going to go to a data base. What is that data base going to be? What is the information going to be?
It is going to look at information on a family unit that is already two years' passe. In the case of a family that does qualify the department is going to send a cheque to whoever filled in the income tax return for that family. In this day and age in Canada imagine, first, the changes in family structures that occur year to year. People have had children added to their families. How will one possibly know? Children will have left the family setting. Families will have broken up. There will be divorce, separation, or death. Who is going to handle this and what is the process?
When we asked the officials of the department they told us that they do not know. There is no provision in the legislation before us.
For example, what will happen if the money is paid in excess of what should be paid? Even more important for poor people, what will happen if insufficient moneys are paid because the government was not aware of what the actual family situation was?
Where will the government find these people and how will it keep track of them as they move around? We know what a transient society we have with people moving about. How does a mother with custody of the children go and get the cheque from her spouse who filled in the income tax return the year before? How are we going to deal with poor people and low income people?
The government does not know because it has not looked into it yet. It is more interested in selling the goods and services tax as a tax proposal than it is in dealing with the real problems it is going to create by implementation.
When this document came out there were a lot of other things that were said in it. For example, one of the obvious advantages that the government has been promoting is that it will replace an existing sales tax that is a silent killer of jobs. At the same time that we were being told that, the government was increasing the federal
Government Orders
sales tax from 9 per cent when it came to office in 1984, to 10 per cent, to 11 per cent, to 12 per cent, to 13.5 per cent.
All through this period this terrible invisible tax which the government talks about so much now had actually doubled the revenue accruing to the Government of Canada from that tax source. We are talking here about lies and misrepresentations, the way people distort and try to convince Canadians that black is white and good is bad, and that what is going to happen to them with the GST is going to be something to bring smiles to their faces.
Imagine at the same time the government going through a process from 1985 to 1988 and saying that it was creating more jobs in the country than have ever been created before. The government went before the people in 1988 and said: "We have created a million-plus jobs". At the same it had nearly doubled the tax rate, as well as doubled the revenue from this federal sales tax that it now says is a silent killer of jobs. You cannot have it three or four different ways.
I have listened to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of State for Finance and others talk about the existing federal sales tax. They have said: "Everybody agrees it is a bad tax". That is about the only truthful thing that has been said in this entire debate. Everybody agrees that the existing federal sales tax is a bad tax.
However, this is where the hook is put in. Then we hear people say that for years there have been royal commissions, task forces, and study groups, and they have all recommended this tax. That is an absolute lie. Never has any royal commission or task force recommended this goods and services tax. Never has a royal commission or any task force recommended a two tiered retail, consumer driven sales tax in Canada. Never has that occurred.
What all of those commissions and task forces said is that we have a problem with the existing federal sales tax. It has 22,000 special cases and circumstances and exemptions and so forth. It is a very thick and difficult document. It does create problems for 70,000 to 80,000 manufacturers in this country. That is a fact that is acceptable.
But no one has said: "Now go out and create a tax monster, a two-tiered administrative nightmare both for government and for business to replace it". No one has said that, and I defy anybody in this House to come forward with any statement by any respected economist,

April 10, 1990
Government Orders
any commission or task force that has ever suggested such a foolhardy thing.
I listened to the Minister of State for Finance today saying: "But why point a finger at us? Forty-eight other countries have done the same thing". I know that the hon. Minister of State for Finance would not intentionally mislead the Flouse, so I want to take this opportunity to clarify that.
Not a single country in the world has a two tiered retail consumer tax-not one. There is a reason for that. It is because it is unmanageable and unfair. It is because it is too complex. It is because when you eliminate a problem from one sector of our economy, which is manufacturing, instead of causing problems for 75,000 manufacturers or so you then cause a problem for 1.6 million to 1.8 million registrants who will have to collect the GST.
When we talk about fairness, how can we possibly discuss a two tiered sales tax in Canada in every province except for Alberta that will require the hiring of at least 4,000 new tax collectors?
As I indicated, the government has been very proficient in putting out all kinds of material. In August of 1989 it came forward with the proposal. At that time it was said clearly by the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister that that was it. It was another one of these take-it-or-leave-it deals that the government likes. The government said: "It is not going to change. We are adamant and we are going ahead".
It turned out that there was a fly in the ointment, and a big one at that. The chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance had already smelled the rat in 1988. In 1988, when the government was running around saying nothing is going to cost you more and everything is going to better and all of these programs that we are putting together in our electoral platform will not cost you a single nickel more, the member for Mississauga South, the chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, ran the flag up the pole and said: "Whoa, that is not so".
That was a very courageous act.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: When did he say that?

In 1988 during the campaign. That is when the member for Mississauga South made a clear statement. Based on his experience and the experience of the committee having looked into the situation in New Zealand and being aware of what had happened in other jurisdictions where the goods and services tax was opposed, the hon. member said: "Just a minute here. You are going to find a lot more money in that goods and services tax than you guys are saying".

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Is that the only Tory who was telling the truth?

He was the only Conservative member at that point who would tell the truth and come straight out and say: "Look, that is just not going to fly because it does not make any sense".
The Conservative member for Mississauga South, the chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, said this. I want to be fair about this since the proposal at that time was for a 9 per cent tax. Whatever the proposal was the member must have known because he made this statement. He estimated that a national sales tax would bring in between $10 billion and $14 billion in additional revenue.
Obviously, that would not be the figure at this point, and I want to be fair to the hon. member, because everyone expected that the rate would be somewhat higher than 7 per cent. Looking at what has happened elsewhere, and this is why I want to come back to what the Minister of State had to say today, you have to question whether or not the government would put itself through this masochistic exercise to maintain revenue neutrality.
What sane human being, what kind of government would do that, after seeing itself so low in the polls? If this continues, and I am not one to make predictions, the rate on the GST will be higher than the popularity rating of the Conservative party in this country.
Why would any government in the face of this unheard of coalition of opposition continue down this path to self-destruction? There has to be a hook, because that is the Tory way. Thank goodness that the experienced member for Mississauga South, the chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, spotted it early and alerted Canadians to the fact that the pot of gold at the
April 10, 1990

end of the GST rainbow is a $4 billion to $5 billion windfall that will help the government on its merry way to try to buy Canadians before the next election and convince them that things are not as bad as they thought they were going to be.
I want to put this in a little bit of perspective. Consider any Canadians putting themselves in the position of the Minister of Finance and saying: "Okay, here we are now, we have Shirley Carr and the Canadian Labour Congress, we have John Bulloch and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, we have the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, senior citizens' organizations, anti-poverty groups, professional organizations and insurance adjusters all opposed to the GST". The list goes on forever.
As a matter of fact, if I can ever get the chance, Mr. Speaker, I have over 100,000 signatures on petitions in my possession from bowlers across this country to table in this Flouse. Imagine, men and women, young and old, people who go out for recreational bowling or competitive bowling taking the trouble to sign documents that have been certified by the Clerk-over 100,000 of them-saying "no" to the GST.
Just imagine the average average Canadian sitting there saying: "I am the Minister of Finance". Why would a person undertake the goods and services tax as it is proposed here? This is the proposal. Bill C-62 is now a package at last. Why would you do it, when some people say, and the documents maintain it, that it is revenue neutral? The Minister of Finance said it is not going to cost Canadians one penny of additional tax. Yet you have got 80 per cent of Canadians outraged. You have got small business in such an angry state of mind that the Minister of Finance has refused to meet John Bulloch now for months and months and months. He will not talk to him, or have anything to do with him, a person who represents some 80,000 Canadian small businesses. All of these people are massively opposed to the GST and here is the government saying: "We are going to continue going ahead with it anyway".
Talking about tax cuts, the government has shut down VIA Rail and laid off people all over the place. It has cut back on programs, closed down shelters for women and cut off funding for information media for aboriginal peoples. The government has done all those things, Mr. Speaker, but then says to the Canadian people, because it wants to be consistent: "In order to collect this
Government Orders
revenue neutral tax that is going to be good for Canadians we are going to hire a minimum of 4,000 new tax collectors, and we are going to hire 250 specialized people who will be tax police. We are going to recruit from the commercial fraud section of the RCMP and anybody who has a background in tax and being able to see through all these problems".
Mr. Speaker, just put yourself in the position of being an ordinary Canadian sitting in your living room saying: "I am going to pretend I am finance minister. So what am I going to do? I am going to put a tax on people that they despise. It is going to turn 80 per cent of Canadians against me. I am not going to have one penny more left after I have gone through all of this exercise. I am going to have 4,000 new tax collectors on my payroll. They are going to be all over the place checking into everybody and all of their dealings. I will not be able to get into a cab because the guy will slam the door on my hand, because I have to have my hand out to collect the GST". So here you are a finance minister who is going to have to walk for the rest of your life or drive your own car.
The finance minister cannot go and get a haircut because, even though there is not too much business now for a shave and a haircut, the barber may decide to give him a shave with a straight-edge razor.
The finance minister cannot go to a movie theatre because he would walk in and the people standing in line would say: "Well, well, well, this is the guy who is costing me an extra 7 per cent to go into a movie theatre."
He cannot go to a hockey game. The finance minister is going to have to become a hermit.
This whole question is going to be part of the Canadian game and there is not much humour in this affair, to say the least. But with Michael H. Wilson you are never sure. Is it "hold-up"? Is it "hermit"? What does that "H" stand for?
The question I want to put to Canadians is: If you were sitting there actually thinking about doing this yourself, would you undertake this perilous journey down the slippery slope of goods and services tax and say: "Not a penny more? Eveiybody is going to be mad at Mike. But I am going to have 4,000 new people on the federal payroll collecting taxes, tormenting people, running around and auditing people, finding out if they are registered, checking the paper trail, doing all the kinds of things that so outraged Canadians not that many years ago with the income tax system". I think that no matter

April 10, 1990
how many pieces of paper the government produces it will not change their mind.
There is so much paper here concerning this tax. It has been one of the most savage attacks on Canadian forests that we have seen in a long time. Not everybody is going to accept this tax. The government has produced all kinds of paper, and we are just at the August documents at this point.
At that point in August, these were the pamphlets, Mr. Speaker, if you can imagine, that the government put out to explain this simple tax. There is information for senior citizens, for barbers and hair-stylists, for convenience stores, for exporters, housing, self-employed tradespeople, farmers and fishermen, information for dealers and used vehicles, information for commission agents, information for tutors and instructors, information for travel agents and tour operators, information for real estate agents, information for students, information for pharmacies and drug marts, information for taxi limousine drivers, information for service station operators, and information for charities.
These are just the booklets to help explain what goes on here. This is just the beginning of this savage attack on the forests of Canada to try to make sure that Canadians understand the goods and services tax.
At the same time, I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that there was a previous document that we missed. This document came out with the 1989 budget.
One of the reasons that Canadians are not too convinced about the goods and services tax is because in 1989 in the budget you may recall, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance was predicting interest rates around 10 per cent by the end of the year.
Mr. Speaker, you could imagine that would throw a few people off when they are looking at other things that are said in here. This document was brought out with the 1989 budget. It misrepresents what the goods and services tax has become because it talks about simplicity, fairness, revenue neutrality and integration.
None of those basic elements has been achieved. That is why, as the government continues on its attempt to try to tell Canadians what is good about the GST, it has even failed, Mr. Speaker, as you well know, to convince
members of the government. That is why we will not have a free vote later on today when we have a vote.
Two people who even decided to exercise minimum freedom have been expelled.
How may free votes did the Liberals have?
I am just listening to the hon. member for South Shore. I know he is upset about this tax.

Before moving on, I wonder if both the hon. member for Gloucester and the hon. member for Dartmouth could see me in my Chambers on the matter that was raised yesterday.
The hon. member for Gloucester has the floor and I would not want to interrupt that, but perhaps at a time convenient to both of them they could come and see me.

Mr. Speaker, I would be more than pleased to meet with Your Honour at a time appropriate and convenient to us all.
To continue, Mr. Speaker, the whole question of dealing with Bill C-62 is a very arduous one. From the very outset the tone was set for the debate in the 1988 election. As we have discussed many times in the past year and half, the credibility of the government is fundamental to whether or not Canadians believe that the goods and services tax is an acceptable proposal.
I think it is fair to say that this proposal did not get off to a very good start when the Minister of Finance characterized our concern about it during the 1988 election campaign by describing the Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada as a liar and a coward. We know how abhorrent those terms are in this House. We have just had some indication of that in the kinds of words that have been uttered back and forth across the floor in this place in the last few minutes.
What is extremely critical for Canadians to recognize is the fact that the government is now telling Canadians that this is the only way to proceed in several areas of major concern that it has identified. The government has told us that the existing federal sales tax is so badly
flawed that there is no alternative but the goods and services tax.
In 1984, I believe that most Canadians were prepared to give the Minister of Finance the benefit of the doubt, when he stated that he was going to involve himself and his government in a major reform of the tax system in this country. Going back again to the legislation, the draft legislation and the technical documents that were brought forward, it is hard to understand where we went astray.
There were a number of aspects to tax reform when the government began the process in 1984. It involved reform of the tax system as it applied to corporate taxes and also for personal taxation. It was our impression and I believe that of Canadians that this was going to come together as a package.
What is actually taking place is that we are asked to deal with this legislation at this time, after a general election, during which time, the Minister of Finance was describing the Leader of the Liberal Party in very unflattering terms. The government at that point was telling Canadians that there would have to be a rate for a national sales tax that would be lower in every province than the existing federal and provincial sales taxes taken together.
Those are the kinds of statements that were made and on which I believe people depended. We are now being told that the goods and services tax was an issue in the 1988 election, and that Canadians have given this government a mandate to deal with the reform of the system by imposing the goods and services tax. Surely, we are beginning to recognize that there is nothing in the goods and services tax proposal, Bill C-62, that remotely resembles what was either promised in 1984 as part of tax reform, or what was talked about during the 1988 election campaign.
I repeat. The Minister of Finance said, and I quote:
The rate of the new national sales tax would be lower in every
province than the existing federal and provincial taxes taken
together.
Except for Alberta, which does not have a provincial sales tax, the imposition of the federal sales tax not only will not result in what that commitment undertook but the provincial sales taxes will be hiked because it is imposed on top of the federal sales tax. So without the provincial governments doing a single thing, we are faced with a situation where not only was this commitment not
April 10, 1990

recognized and adhered to, provincial government sales taxes will be increased because of the cascading effect.
I listen often to members of the government talking about alternatives, and that you have to put forward alternatives. Let us call a spade a spade. The government has had since 1984 to put forward an alternative to the federal sales tax. It has come up with a tax that 80 per cent of Canadians are opposed to.
I want to be very clear that there are groups which have consistently opposed the federal sales tax. They are convinced, as are many Canadians, of the difficulties inherent in the federal sales tax, such as the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce, at its annual meeting in Saint John, New Brunswick, last fall stated that as bad as the federal sales tax is, unless it was changed and basic requirements and conditions for change were made, then the government should stick with the federal sales tax until it can get this proposal put together properly to let real tax reform take place.
I want to make sure that Canadians understand that the red herring we are being given of there being no alternative, is just that. The Chamber of Commerce-I do not want to misrepresent its position-do believe that the FST should be replaced. It even believes in the principle of the goods and services tax which we in the Liberal party oppose, but the Chamber of Commerce, having taken that position over a number of years, have said to the government and the Standing Committee on Finance as recently as this year, that with the existing proposal, it would recommend to every member of the House of Commons that they vote against the goods and services tax, Bill C-62.
How can we possibly accept the approach of the government members that everyone who is opposed to the goods and services tax is opposed to it either for partisan or political reasons, or doesn't understand it? That was the attitude taken last fall when the goods and services tax was being considered by the Standing Committee on Finance and we travelled across the country.
We went into Alberta and Albertans were told by the standing committee chairman that they were so uninformed about the tax-the actual word used was so
Government Orders
"ignorant" about the tax-that grade five teachers from Ontario should be sent west to educate westerners on the goods and services tax. I think it was a monumental mistake for the chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance to say that because those Albertans who perhaps did not understand the tax have taken up the issue and have learned enough about it to make sure that they know they are totally opposed to it.
But what particularly irritated Albertans was the cavalier attitude taken by members of the government toward the serious reservations put forward by the premier of Alberta, the hon. Mr. Getty, and his treasurer, the hon. Mr. Johnston.
This is not unheard of but it is extremely unusual in this country to have the Conservative premier of Alberta and the Conservative treasurer of Alberta being told implicitly by government members that they do not understand, that their opposition to the goods and services tax is ill-founded.
Beyond that, to put a little salt in the wound, government members have stated, the Minister of Finance and officials of his department have also said, that Alberta will be better off than any other province in Canada after the imposition of the GST. Imagine the kind of guff that the government is trying to peddle in Alberta.
Here is a government that commissioned its own study. The Government of Alberta commissioned a study released before the end of the year, in which it clearly set out its position that the goods and services tax would have a very negative and serious effect on Alberta. It would cause problems in a number of areas, such as the service industries, the resource-based industries, the tourist industry and will affect disposable income.
So, Mr. Speaker, here we have this very unusual situation of us, to your left, being told by government members, that we do not understand the tax, and that we are doing it because we are exploiting-to quote the Minister of State for Finance-"for political purposes" the fears of people by setting out the GST as a terrible burden on Canadians.
Following a study commissioned by the government of Alberta, and paid for by the taxpayers of Alberta, the premier and treasurer of Alberta have said that the goods and services tax will be a terrible burden on

April 10, 1990

economic activity and the social well-being of the people of Alberta.
The basic question is, who are we to believe? I want to be very clear on this. I have been to Alberta more than once. Everywhere I go people I meet are aware that I am a Liberal. I would not be offended, and I mean this, to be in Alberta and to have people say: "Well, you know Doug Young from northern New Brunswick, a little town called Tracadie, is out here telling us that the goods and services tax is a bad thing for us". They probably would not be very upset with the fact that I am from Tracadie, but they would be very upset with the fact that I am a Liberal. It is a fact of life in Alberta that it can cause you some grief in terms of credibility to go out and tell people that you are a Liberal representing this party and that you come from the east.
If I were the one who was putting forward this premise, I could accept that people would have some reservations. On the weekend the Premier of Alberta, in convention, faced extremely serious questions about the future of this country. I do not want in this place at this time to get into that. I think Canadians from coast to coast were proud of the fact that Albertans and their government stood up for Canada. Surely, I am proud of that.
Hear, hear!

At the same time the Government of Alberta was faced with having to deal with its colleagues in Ottawa imposing a goods and services tax. I do not want to focus entirely on Alberta. I use it because it best exemplifies the dichotomy that exists in this country from the point of view of Conservatives. Here you are with a party in government, a party which has been there for a long time with Mr. Getty and his predecessor Premier Lougheed, in full open convention dealing with major national issues such as national unity and the economy with the leadership of the premier having been reaffirmed unequivocally, and we have people who have the audacity to say in this place and outside of it that Liberals and members of the New Democratic Party oppose the goods and services tax for partisan reasons.
Canadians have to understand that if Premier Getty and Treasurer Johnston oppose the goods and services
tax, surely it cannot be for partisan reasons. Surely it must be because they understand better than anyone what the impact will be on the economy of their province.
I ask Canadians as we continue dealing with what this government wants to do to them with respect to the imposition of the GST to remember not to question the motives of those who point out the difficulties with the goods and services tax, but to question the motives of those who insist that they have seen the light and that their view of the affair is the only one to take and if you do not take it there is something wrong with you. Never argue it on merit. Always try to colour it and play it with smoke and mirrors. It is revenue neutral, but it is going to be a deficit reduction tool. Even I am boggled at times when I start to think about the way the Tories approach Bill C-62, because it does get very convoluted.
Going back to the question of alternatives Canadians have to understand that the Alberta government put forward in its study a clear process that it believes should be followed.
First, it insisted that there had to be meaningful tax reform. That is a situation that I believe we must address when we are talking about the goods and services tax. There is a feeling in the country now that the FST has to go, and surely it should go at an appropriate time when an appropriate tax package is put together. The Government of Alberta in rejecting the goods and services tax did not rush out and say: "This is what we should do specifically".
